## The Lithosphere and Plate Motion
Let's start with two easy ideas. Earth's outer rocky layer is called the lithosphere. It is not one solid shell. It is broken into many pieces, like tiles fitted together. The material calls this a mosaic.
Each piece is a tectonic plate. A tectonic plate is one of these large, rigid pieces of the lithosphere. The plates float on a layer below them called the asthenosphere. The asthenosphere is ductile. That means it can slowly flow, like thick putty. The plates slide over it.
Quick check: type the name of the layer the plates float on.
Why do plates move? Three reasons. One: mantle convection, which is slow churning of hot rock. Two: slab pull, which means a sinking plate edge pulls the rest of the plate. Three: ridge push, which means raised ridges push plates apart. The speeds are small: centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹). That is about how fast fingernails grow.
Here is the same idea in a picture:
mantle convection -> hot rock churns slowly
slab pull -> sinking edge pulls plate
ridge push -> raised ridge pushes plates apart
Quick check: type one of the three reasons plates move.
Plates meet at boundaries. A boundary is where two plates touch. There are three kinds:
Divergent: plates pull apart -> normal-fault earthquakes, shallow depths
Convergent: plates collide -> thrust-fault earthquakes, deep to shallow
Transform: plates slide past -> strike-slip earthquakes, shallow to intermediate
Quick check: at which boundary type do plates collide? Type the name.
Worked example: Say a plate edge is locked by friction. Friction means surfaces grip each other so they cannot slide. Step 1: the plates keep moving, so stress builds up at the locked edge. Step 2: strain builds in the rock. Strain is the stretching or bending of rock under stress. Step 3: the strain grows until it exceeds rock strength. Exceeds means it goes past the limit. Step 4: the rock snaps loose, and an earthquake happens. This is why earthquakes cluster at boundaries instead of being spread out everywhere.
Many people think earthquakes happen in random places, anywhere at all. That idea fails because plate edges are locked by friction, so stress piles up in those exact spots. The right idea: earthquakes trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions. Kinematic framework just means the map of where and how plates move against each other.
Quick check from earlier: is the asthenosphere rigid or ductile? Type the word.
Why do boundaries get so much slip? Three more reasons from the material. Fault geometry: pre-existing faults concentrate slip. A fault is a crack where rock can slide. Rheological contrast: cold, brittle lithosphere borders warm, ductile mantle, focusing deformation. Deformation means rock changing shape. Geometric incompatibility: curved plate margins force localized shear zones. Localized means gathered in one small area.
Now try one on your own, at your own pace. There is no rush and nothing to worry about. In your words, type why e

## Plate Speeds and Worked Examples
Let's start with plate speed. The Pacific Plate moves northwest at about 5 cm per year. The Nazca Plate slides under South America at about 8 cm per year. These fast speeds bring many large earthquakes to the Circum-Pacific 'Ring of Fire.'
A picture of the speeds: Pacific Plate → 5 cm/yr (northwest) Nazca Plate → 8 cm/yr (subducting) One centimeter per year means the plate moves 1 centimeter in one year. That is about the width of your fingernail.
Quick check (just type your answer, no pressure): which plate moves faster, the Pacific Plate or the Nazca Plate?
Worked example: let's use the seismic cycle to describe one big earthquake at a subduction zone. Step 1: Interseismic. The locked zone stores strain for decades to centuries. Step 2: Coseismic. Sudden slip releases the stored energy in seconds to minutes. Step 3: Postseismic. Afterslip and slow relaxation move stress around for months to years. Step 4: Preseismic. Possible warning signs may appear, like foreshocks or slow slip. So the cycle runs: store strain → sudden slip → slow adjustment → possible warning signs.
Now try one with the last step left for you. A segment has not ruptured in a full cycle. What does seismic gap theory say about it? Type your answer, then compare it with the key points below.
Now earthquake depth. Shallow events, 10 km deep or less, happen at ridges and transform faults. Deeper events, 30 to 300 km, happen in the Wadati-Benioff zone. That zone is inside a sinking slab at a subduction zone.
A subduction earthquake at 30 km depth gets its energy from two sources: bending of the crust, and water leaving the slab (slab dehydration).
Quick check: at what depth range do deeper events happen? Type the two numbers.

Postseismic – afterslip and slow relaxation move stress around (months to years) 4. Preseismic – possible warning signs, like foreshocks or slow slip
One more idea: seismic gap theory. A segment that has not ruptured in a full cycle is a candidate for a future large event. Scientists also use GPS and InSAR to measure plate speeds in cm per year and improve coupling models.
Watch out: a quiet segment is not a safe segment. The passage warns that a segment with no rupture in a full cycle may be the next place for a large event.
Why it matters: these plate speeds explain why large earthquakes happen so often along the Ring of Fire. Hazard assessment uses this to find candidate segments for future large events.
In other words: fast plates store strain quickly, sudden slip lets it out, and quiet segments may be the next to break.
One point to recall tomorrow: fast plates (Pacific ≈ 5 cm/yr, Nazca ≈ 8 cm/yr) store strain quickly, and unruptured segments are candidates for the next large event.

## The Seismic Cycle at a Convergent Margin

The seismic cycle has four stages. Here they are as a chain:
interseismic (strain builds) → coseismic (sudden slip) → postseismic (afterslip, relaxation) → back to interseismic
Before a big event, there may be preseismic signals. These are foreshocks and slow slip.
In words: first, the locked zone builds up strain. This takes decades or centuries. Strain means stored elastic energy, like a stretched spring. Then sudden slip happens in seconds to minutes. The stored energy is released as an earthquake. After that, afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation move stress around. This takes months to years. Afterslip is slow sliding after the main slip. Finally, warning signals may appear before a big event.
In symbols: interseismic → coseismic → postseismic → (possible preseismic signals) → interseismic ...
Quick check: which stage lasts months to years? Type it from memory.
---
Worked example: let's walk through the four stages for one earthquake. We use only what the lesson says.
Step 1 — Interseismic: the locked zone builds up strain. This takes decades to centuries. Picture a spring being stretched slowly.
Step 2 — Coseismic: sudden slip happens. It takes seconds to minutes. The stored elastic energy is released as an earthquake.
Step 3 — Postseismic: afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation move stress around. Afterslip is slow sliding after the main slip. This takes months to years.
Step 4 — Back to interseismic: the cycle starts again. Strain builds once more. If signals come before a big event, they are preseismic: foreshocks and slow slip.
Now you try the last step. After postseismic finishes, which stage comes next? What happens there? Type your answer.
